description: We are MindSync, a team of 6 passionate and ambitious innovators united by our interest in space, technology, and innovation. Our team combines diverse skills in AI, machine learning, coding, software development, data analysis, visualization, design, and communication. Driven by creativity, collaboration, and problem-solving, we aim to transform bold ideas into impactful solutions and push the boundaries of innovation through the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary: In space, stopping a fan does not necessarily stop a fire. EMBER turns NASA microgravity combustion data into a traceable evidence workspace for researchers, students and aerospace teams. Built by MindSync, the prototype brings together 129 BASS-II experimental-table records, nine Saffire publication records and twelve source-linked findings. Users can explore experiments, compare materials and atmospheric conditions, retrieve relevant observations, and identify where a proposed scenario exceeds the available evidence. A demonstration follows a Saffire cotton flame that recovered after a 70-second fan-off interval, then shows why microgravity results cannot automatically be applied to a lunar habitat. EMBER addresses Flame in Freefall by making combustion evidence easier to inspect and interpret without hiding its limitations. Its local retrieval engine works without a paid API. The intended impact is better-informed research and fewer unsupported comparisons; scientific validation remains a next step.
details:
The problem

In NASA’s Saffire V-2 experiment, a cotton flame recovered when airflow returned after a 70-second fan-off interval. This observation challenges a simple assumption: stopping ventilation does not always guarantee extinction. However, its meaning depends on the material, atmosphere and experimental history.

NASA combustion experiments contain valuable evidence, but interpreting that evidence requires keeping results connected to their original conditions. EMBER helps users make those connections.

Our solution

EMBER is a microgravity fire evidence workspace developed for MindSync’s Flame in Freefall entry. It organizes research into four actions: explore experiments, compare conditions, retrieve findings and identify evidence gaps.

The experiment explorer provides access to 129 original BASS-II experimental-table records from NASA PSI-25, including original fields and data-review flags. NASA PSI-98 metadata and its original Saffire-I table are also preserved.

The prototype includes nine distinct Saffire test records transcribed from Tables 1 and 2 of NASA-hosted paper ICES-2021-266. Six contain measured steady and maximum flame sizes.

How it works

The comparison view displays experimental measurements alongside material, oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow and geometry. For example, comparing Saffire IV-1 and V-2 highlights changes in material, oxygen and pressure. This prevents users from attributing the entire difference in flame size to oxygen alone.

The evidence assistant uses local TF-IDF cosine retrieval to rank twelve curated scientific findings. Each result includes its source and experimental scope. It retrieves documented summaries rather than generating new physical predictions.

The evidence-gap view compares a proposed scenario with available Saffire records. It flags missing material or gravity coverage and conditions outside the collection’s ranges. Its similarity score is a transparent heuristic, not a probability of fire or a safety rating. Users can export a research evidence brief.

Creativity and intended impact

EMBER makes the limits of evidence visible alongside the findings. A hypothetical lunar scenario illustrates this approach: similar atmospheric conditions do not make a microgravity result a validated lunar prediction.

The intended users are students, combustion researchers and aerospace R&D teams reviewing experimental evidence. The proposed benefit is easier access to relevant observations and fewer unsupported comparisons. These benefits remain to be measured through user studies and scientific review.

Tools and implementation

The application uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Python supported data preparation, while Node.js supported automated checks. Presentation and document preparation used OpenAI Artifact Tool and ReportLab.

The prototype runs locally without a paid API or specialized hardware. Original CSV files, normalized data, source versions and SHA-256 hashes are included.

Missing values remain missing. Questionable readings are preserved and flagged. BASS instrument settings are not presented as calibrated airflow speeds. Publication values and PSI values remain separate where labels or rounding differ.

Validation and next steps

Fifteen authored automated checks passed for data retention, selected retrieval cases, comparison logic and evidence-gap behavior. These checks are not an independent performance benchmark.

Next steps include independent transcription review, assessment by combustion specialists, a held-out retrieval evaluation and expansion to additional NASA datasets, including smoke and suppression research.

Use of SI and project limitations

ChatGPT assisted ideation, research, data transcription and interpretation, coding, debugging, testing, writing, visual design and presentation preparation.

The running application uses deterministic information retrieval, not a live large language model or a trained combustion predictor. Original NASA measured values were not replaced by synthetic data. The BASS photograph is source imagery credited to NASA/Space Apps, not an SI-generated image.

EMBER is a research prototype, not a flight-certified system or emergency procedure. No NASA endorsement, operational spacecraft deployment or predictive accuracy is claimed.
